facts.raw_span: a 4-month history of severe occipital and temporal headaches
headaches that were paroxysmal, aggravated by changes in position
associated with bilateral blurry vision and morning projectile vomiting
a kinetic and static cerebellar syndrome with ataxia, imbalance, uncoordinated movements, bilateral nystagmus, and stage I bilateral papilledema
Routine blood tests were unremarkable
Noncontrast CT of the head showed no abnormalities
an inferior median oval lesion of the cerebellar vermis measuring 40 × 31 × 29 mm
hypointense on T1-weighted images, heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images
heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium administration
the lesion filled the foramen of Magendie, exerted mass effect on the medulla
no surrounding edema on FLAIR
elevated choline peak and reduced N-acetyl aspartate signal

concepts.why: The patient's cerebellar syndrome, the location and appearance of the lesion on MRI, and the spectroscopy findings are consistent with medulloblastoma.
The patient's cerebellar lesion with heterogeneous enhancement and mass effect on the medulla could be consistent with hemangioblastoma.
The patient's cerebellar syndrome and the appearance of the lesion on MRI could be consistent with pilocytic astrocytoma.
The patient's cerebellar lesion with heterogeneous enhancement and mass effect on the medulla could be consistent with ependymoma.
The patient's cerebellar syndrome and the appearance of the lesion on MRI could be consistent with atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor.

rationales.F04: Cerebellar syndrome is common in cerebellar tumors
rationales.F07: Inferior median oval lesion of the cerebellar vermis is suggestive of medulloblastoma
rationales.F12: Elevated choline peak and reduced N-acetyl aspartate signal are characteristic of high-grade tumors like medulloblastoma

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's presentation with a kinetic and static cerebellar syndrome, ataxia, and an inferior median oval lesion of the cerebellar vermis, along with the imaging characteristics of the lesion being hypointense on T1-weighted images and heterogeneously hyperintense on T2-weighted images with heterogeneous enhancement, are most consistent with a pilocytic astrocytoma, which is a common cerebellar tumor in adults that can present with these features.
